newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: UNICEF chief says gap widens between rich and poor.
newsitem.headline: UNICEF chief says gap widens between rich and poor.

text.p: Poverty kills about 12 million children a year and the globalization of the world economy has done little, if anything, to stop it, Carol Bellamy, UNICEF's executive director, said on Wednesday.

"In some ways, with the globalization of the economy, the focus has been on economic investment," Bellamy told Reuters. "We certainly are not against that but it has been without adequate investment on the human development side."

Bellamy, a former director of the U.S. Peace Corps, marks her third anniversary as head of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) on Thursday. She spoke about the job and some of the most serious problems facing the world's children in an interview on the sidelines of a regional UNICEF meeting here.

She said enormous progress had been made in providing children with basic health and education services over the past decade and noted that "infant mortality rates have been cut in half in the last 25 years." But she stressed "there are about 12 million children who die each year from preventable reasons," and all them stem from poverty.

"It's not a particular kind of disease, it's not a particular war, it's poverty," she said of the leading killer of children worldwide. "It's poverty whether its the furthest rural village you've ever been to or the barrio just down the street."

On the issue of what she terms "the utilization of available resources," Bellamy said "there's still too much money put into arms and the military" while too little was being spent on developing people as a whole.

Without spending on education and other public services, she said, globalization was unlikely to yield long-term economic strength in developing countries and most would be condemned to an ever-widening gap between rich and poor.

"There's more wealth in the world today but with that greater wealth comes greater disparity," said Bellamy, who spent half her adult life as a corporate lawyer and investment banker. "What's getting worse is the disparity between those that have and those that do not have."

Despite what she described as the increasing use of children in armed conflicts, and estimates that about 250 million children aged five to 14 are subjected to some form of child labour, Bellamy said there was progress on many fronts.

"We will go into the next century with a dramatically improved profile of conditions for children in the world," she said, but poverty, war and the rapid spread of AIDS were leading "restrictors" to a better world for children.
